title: The Backward Footprints of the Ciguapa
premise: A night hunter discovers the cursed tracks of the mountain forest spirit.
central_question: Why do the forest tracks appear to run forward then backward?
understanding_shift: The reversed tracks are caused by the ciguapa’s backward‑facing feet.
ending_payoff: So the reversed footprints were her backward feet, the mark of a ciguapa.
viewer_lesson: After watching, the viewer can explain that the earliest written account of the ciguapa is the 1866 story La Ciguapa by Francisco Javier Angulo Guridi, and that the legend’s backward feet create the puzzling tracks.
call_to_action: If your town has a similar forest spirit, tell us where and how it goes.

described as nude woman with knee‑length hair and back‑footed
has siren‑like powers of attraction and can seduce men at night
lives in forests and rivers of the mountains of El Cibao
malevolence varies: spirit, jealous, or cannibal
first written account 1866 by Francisco Javier Angulo Guridi in "La Ciguapa"
origin disputed: Taíno mythology or fakelore
used by Trujillo regime as mestizaje propaganda
later re‑contextualized as multicultural feminist icon
beautiful Ciguayo woman, golden skin, almond‑shaped black eyes, three feet tall, carries walking stick
cannot speak, only howl
jealous of human romance, howls causing same‑gender person to die of fright, then dies of sorrow
later legends add backward‑facing feet and seduction of opposite sex
skin tone varies: indigenous, mestizo, Afro‑Dominican, sometimes blue
activities: nocturnal, jump trees, steal crops, forage fruit/fish, ride horses at dawn
lair: trees, grottos, caves, rivers in El Cibao
back‑footed tracks confuse pursuers
hunting dogs required: wild (jíbaro), polydactyl, or black‑haired five‑legged
ciguapa dies quickly when confined
ciguapa term existed earlier for Cuban Stygian owl described 1839
town named La Ciguapa in Oriente Province, Cuba
